theory.title: What is a planetary analog?
theory.text: A terrestrial (planetary) analog is a place on Earth whose conditions resemble, in some specific respect, those of another planetary body — geology, landforms, climate, isolation or operations. No site matches every aspect; analogs are useful for a defined purpose (science, technology testing or crew operations).

theory.title: Why 8 dimensions
theory.text: The site rates every place on eight dimensions — geology, terrain, atmosphere/aeolian, temperature/extremes, water/ice, biology/habitability, subsurface and operational — so that a site can be a strong analog in one respect and weak in another. [TEAM TO FILL: paste the official challenge text that motivates these dimensions, with the link to the 2026 challenge page.]

theory.title: Why missions (landing, rover, base) and not just similarity
theory.text: Analog sites are chosen for what they will be used for. A landing test needs low slopes and a firm surface; a rover test needs varied slopes and obstacles; a base simulation needs isolation and an extreme climate. The same place can be excellent for one mission and useless for another, so the map is organized by planet × mission and each rule is explained on the card.

theory.title: Novelty as a criterion
theory.text: Most analog work concentrates on a few classic regions (Atacama, Devon Island, Iceland, Hawai'i, Antarctica). The validation score rewards well-documented proposals more than 25 km from any known site, outside those regions, to help surface new candidates — for example the Brazilian impact craters.

theory.title: Where Earth falls short
theory.text: No place on Earth reproduces the Moon's ~1/6 g or Mars' ~3/8 g, the lunar vacuum or Mars' thin CO2 atmosphere, or the surface radiation environment beyond Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere. Earth also has a biosphere almost everywhere, which complicates life-detection tests. The radiation gap is shown with real numbers from NASA RadLab (ISS dose rate) next to the natural background on Earth.

mapStates.rule: sites.json has a history entry for the same planet and mission (a known test of that type).
No such history entry, but the site passes every REQUIRED rule of criteria.json for that planet × mission (partial is allowed).
A required rule fails. The site still exists in the data and may appear on other maps.
NASA data contradicts a hand-entered attribute or a required rule (DATA-CHECK.md). Never changed automatically — the team decides.

method.indicatorsIntro: Measured NASA values become suggested levels with the thresholds below. They are PROJECT RULES chosen by the team for the prototype, not scientific consensus.

method.scoreWarning: Community check against NASA open data — not peer review.

items: Code: the site's HTML/CSS/JavaScript, the Python pre-computation scripts and the data-check logic were generated with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code, by Anthropic) and reviewed and tested by the team.
Texts: interface texts, documentation (README, DECISIONS, METHODOLOGY, this page) and first drafts of site descriptions were written with AI assistance.
Sample data: the leaderboard sample contributions (nicknames 'Sample_…', labelled 'Sample data (prototype)') and the two example community submissions are AI-generated and fictional.
Fictional profiles: the archived v1 simulation contained fictional researcher profiles; they are not used in this version.
Research support: AI agents searched for and checked sources (Crossref, CMR, official pages). Only items whose links or DOIs were actually opened are marked verified.
No NASA logos, images of people or AI-generated imagery are used. All imagery comes from NASA GIBS and Solar System Treks.
